issues.legal_issue: Additional evidence may be received in an appeal when it is materially relevant to the issues and is needed for a complete and effective adjudication.
material_facts: In a civil appeal, the respondent sought to produce official records and public documents concerning the extent of the land and the parties’ competing claims to ownership or possession.
If proved, the documents could materially affect the issues and assist the appellate court in pronouncing judgment.
The documents were not in the respondent’s control or possession, and the High Court considered them necessary to determine the parties’ rights.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in allowing the applications for additional evidence; the proposed evidence could be received subject to proof.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XLI Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, additional evidence is not available as of right and may be admitted only within the statutory conditions, including where it is required by the appellate court to pronounce judgment or where the interests of justice make its admission imperative. The court must consider the evidence’s relevance, why it was not previously produced, the applicant’s diligence, and the need for it, and must give reasons. The Court applied Union of India v. Ibrahim Uddin, (2012) 8 SCC 148.

predicates.civil_appeal_with_additional_evidence_re: A party in a civil appeal asks the appellate court to receive evidence that was not produced earlier.
predicates.evidence_material_to_main_issues: The proposed evidence, if established, could materially affect the central issues in the case.
predicates.evidence_needed_for_appellate_judgment: The appellate court needs the proposed evidence to decide the issues and pronounce judgment effectively.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal involves a request for further evidence that could materially affect the central issues and is needed for the appellate judgment, admission of that evidence is justified.

issues.legal_issue: Permission to receive additional documentary evidence does not itself establish the documents or make them admissible as exhibits without proof.
material_facts: The High Court allowed the applications to produce additional documents but stated that the documents would be subject to proof.
The respondent intended to rely on the documents, and their existence, authenticity, genuineness, and contents had not been established merely by allowing the applications.
issues.conclusion: The documents could not be exhibited automatically; the party relying on them had to prove their existence, authenticity, genuineness, and contents as required by law.
issues.legal_principle: An order allowing additional evidence under Order XLI Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits the evidence to be tendered; it does not dispense with the ordinary requirements of proof. The party relying on documents must establish their existence, authenticity, genuineness, and contents as required by law.

predicates.additional_documents_received_for_consid: An appellate court has permitted documents not previously produced to be brought into the appeal for consideration.
predicates.a_party_relies_on_those_documents: A party asks the court to rely on the documents in deciding the dispute.

issues.definition: When documents are received in an appeal and a party relies on them, that party must prove them as required by law.

issues.legal_issue: When further evidence is needed in a second appeal, the High Court should not direct a fresh decision of the entire suit by the trial court without a proper basis for retrial, and may instead have the first appellate court take the evidence and return findings.
material_facts: The High Court was hearing a second appeal from a decree of the first appellate court and allowed additional evidence to be produced.
The High Court sent the parties back to the trial court to decide the suit afresh, but gave no distinct reason why the entire suit had to be retried.
The first appellate court could take the additional evidence and return it with findings, while the High Court retained the second appeal for decision on the substantial questions of law.
issues.conclusion: The direction to the trial court to re-decide the suit was set aside. The High Court was directed to specify the points for the additional evidence, have the first appellate court take that evidence and return it with findings and reasons, and then decide the second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI Rules 23 and 23-A of the Code of Civil Procedure permit remand in the circumstances specified there; the Karnataka amendment to Rule 23 also permits remand where the appellate court considers it necessary in the interests of justice. Rules 25, 28, and 29 provide alternatives, including referring issues for findings and directing the court from whose decree the appeal was preferred to take evidence on specified points and return it. A direction for a full retrial must have a proper basis. The Court relied on H.P. Vedavyasachar v. Shivashankara, (2009) 8 SCC 231, and Shanti Devi v. Daropti Devi, (2006) 13 SCC 775.

predicates.second_appeal_from_first_appellate_decre: The proceeding is a second appeal from a decree made by a first appellate court.
predicates.additional_evidence_requires_fact_findin: The proposed further evidence requires factual assessment or findings before the appeal can be decided.
predicates.independent_retrial_basis: There is a distinct reason, apart from receiving and assessing the further evidence, that requires the entire suit to be retried.

issues.definition: In a second appeal requiring factual findings on further evidence, if no distinct basis requires a full retrial, the evidence should be taken through the first appellate court and returned with findings.
